# Missing Data and Coded Missingness {#sec-missing-data}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```

Not every missing value is a null. In survey, clinical, and administrative data, a missing value is
often recorded as a code, such as `-99` for "not asked" or `-98` for "the respondent refused". If
you treat these codes as ordinary numbers, they will distort any average or sum you compute. If you
recognize them for what they are, they tell you something useful, because the reason a value is
missing can matter as much as the fact that it is missing.

This chapter shows how to validate coded missing values. In Pointblank, you describe a column's
missing-value codes once, in a `MissingSpec`, and then you can ask two kinds of questions. The
first is how much of the column is missing, counting plain nulls, codes, or both. The
`col_pct_null()` and `col_pct_missing()` methods handle that. The second is whether the codes
themselves are used correctly, which is what `col_missing_coded()`, `col_missing_only_coded()`, and
`col_missing_consistent()` check.

We use a small survey table throughout. It has ten respondents and a mix of real values, documented
missing codes, one plain null, and one undocumented code, so each check has something to find.

```{python}
survey = pl.DataFrame({
    "respondent_id": list(range(1, 11)),
    "age":           [34, -98, 41, None, 29, -99, 55, 38, -97, 45],
    "score":         [10, 20, -95, 30, -99, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80],
    "income_source": [1200, -99, 3400, -99, 2100, 5000, -99, 1800, 2600, 3100],
    "income_amount": [1200, -99, 3400, 900, 2100, 5000, -99, 1800, 2600, 3100],
})

pb.preview(survey, n_head=10, n_tail=0)
```

The `age` column has real ages alongside the codes `-98`, `-99`, and `-97`, plus one plain null
for respondent 4. The `score` column has a `-95` that is not a documented code. We will use the two
income columns to check a skip pattern later on. First, though, we need to tell Pointblank what the
codes mean.

## When missing values carry meaning

A null only tells you that a value is absent. A missing-value code tells you why it is absent, and
in many fields that difference matters. An income left blank because the question was never asked
is not the same as an income left blank because the respondent refused to answer, and an analysis
that treats them the same throws away information that someone deliberately recorded. Statistical
software has supported this idea for a long time. SAS, SPSS, and Stata each have their own
conventions for special missing values, and clinical data standards define a detailed set of
"null flavors".


The trouble is that these codes are usually stored as ordinary numbers. A `-99` in an age column
will pull an average down, and a range check that expects ages from 0 to 120 will flag it as an
error rather than recognizing it as a documented non-response. To validate coded missing values
properly, you first tell Pointblank which values are codes, so it can treat them separately from the
real data.

## Describing missingness with `MissingSpec`

A `MissingSpec` describes a column's missing-value codes. The main part is the `reasons=` mapping,
which pairs each code with the reason it stands for. You can also group reasons into `categories=`,
and the `null_is_missing=` flag controls whether a plain null counts as missing along with the codes
(it does by default). The spec for our survey lists three codes and groups two of them.

```{python}
spec = pb.MissingSpec(
    reasons={-99: "not_asked", -98: "refused", -97: "dont_know"},
    categories={"item_nonresponse": ["refused", "dont_know"]},
)
```

This says that `-99`, `-98`, and `-97` are documented missing codes with the given meanings, and
that "refused" and "dont_know" together form a category called `item_nonresponse`. Survey
researchers often care about this grouping, because both reasons mean the respondent was asked but
chose not to answer, which is different from never being asked.

With a spec in hand, we can go back to the range check problem from the previous section. Most of
the `col_vals_*` methods from @sec-column-validations accept a `missing=` argument, and passing the
spec tells the check to set the codes aside. Here is an age range check on the survey, first without the spec and then with it.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_vals_between(columns="age", left=0, right=120)
    .col_vals_between(columns="age", left=0, right=120, missing=spec)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Without the spec, the first step has six passes and four failures: the three codes, which fall
outside the range, and the null. With `missing=spec`, all ten rows pass. The codes are recognized
as documented missing values, and so is the null, since `null_is_missing=` defaults to `True`. The
range check can now focus on the real ages, and the rest of this chapter covers how to check the
missing values themselves.

Since some fields follow well-known standards for missing-value codes, Pointblank can also build a
spec for you. The `MissingSpec.from_cdisc()` constructor produces the HL7 and CDISC null flavors,
and `MissingSpec.from_sas()` and `MissingSpec.from_spss()` produce the conventions of those
statistical packages. For example, if a file exported from SPSS declares certain negative numbers
as user-missing, `from_spss()` turns that declaration into a spec.

```{python}
spss_spec = pb.MissingSpec.from_spss(missing_values=[-1, -2, -3])
spss_spec.reasons
```

Each declared value gets a generated reason label (`"missing_1"`, `"missing_2"`, and
`"missing_3"`). The `from_sas()` constructor works the same way for the SAS special missing values,
mapping `.` and `._` to `"system_missing"` and `.A` through `.Z` to `"user_missing_a"` through
`"user_missing_z"`. The CDISC version is covered in @sec-clinical-cdisc. For the rest of this
chapter we use our own `spec`, since the survey uses its own codes rather than a package convention.

## Measuring how much is missing

The first question about a column is usually how much of it is missing. Once codes are involved,
there are two ways to count. One is the plain null rate, which ignores codes. The other counts codes
and nulls together. Pointblank has a method for each, and both produce a single test unit for the
whole column.

### The null rate with `col_pct_null`

The `col_pct_null()` method checks the proportion of nulls against an expected value `p=`, with an
optional `tol=` for a tolerance. It ignores the codes completely and counts only nulls. The `age`
column has one null out of ten rows, a rate of 0.1.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_pct_null(columns="age", p=0.1)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The single test unit passes, because the null rate is exactly 0.1. Checking for a specific null
rate might seem odd, since we usually want fewer nulls, not a particular number. For an optional
field, though, a stable rate is often what you want to confirm. If about 10 percent of respondents
normally skip a question and suddenly 80 percent do, something has changed in how the data is
collected. If you want no nulls at all, use `p=0.0`. That check would fail here, since the column
has one null.

An exact rate is usually too strict, because a real column changes a little from run to run without
anything being wrong. The `tol=` argument turns the expected value into a range, and any rate within
`tol` of `p` passes. With a tolerance of 0.05 around 0.1, the check passes easily.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_pct_null(columns="age", p=0.1, tol=0.05)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The check passes, and it would keep passing as long as the null rate stayed between 0.05 and 0.15.
If we instead expected a rate of 0.2 with the same tolerance, using
`col_pct_null(columns="age", p=0.2, tol=0.05)`, the check would fail, because 0.1 is below the lower
end of the range at 0.15.

### The structured missing rate with `col_pct_missing`

The `col_pct_missing()` method counts both codes and nulls. Given a `MissingSpec`, it counts the
coded values and, because `null_is_missing=` is `True` by default, the nulls as well. It then checks
that the combined rate is at or below `max_pct=`. The `age` column has three codes and one null, so
four out of ten values are missing.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_pct_missing(columns="age", missing=spec, max_pct=0.5)
    .interrogate()
)
```

The check passes, because a missing rate of 0.4 is below the 0.5 limit. A stricter `max_pct=0.3`
would fail. This method can also count a single reason or category. Passing `reason="refused"`
counts only the `-98` values, a rate of 0.1, which passes with `max_pct=0.2`. Passing
`category="item_nonresponse"` counts the refusals and don't-knows together.


## Validating the coding

Knowing how much is missing is only half the job. The other half is checking that missing values are
recorded correctly. The three methods in this section work row by row, so each produces one test
unit per row and shows you exactly which records break the rules.

### Requiring coded absence with `col_missing_coded`

The `col_missing_coded()` method checks that every missing value uses a documented code. A real
value passes and a documented code passes, but a plain null fails, because a null is a missing value
with no reason attached. If your data is supposed to code every missing value, a null means someone
skipped that step.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_missing_coded(columns="age", missing=spec)
    .interrogate()
)
```

Nine of the ten rows pass and one fails. The failing row is respondent 4, whose `age` is a plain
null rather than one of the documented codes. Use this check when your rule is that every missing
value must have a reason.

### Catching undocumented codes with `col_missing_only_coded`

The `col_missing_only_coded()` method checks something different. It asks whether every value is
either a documented code or a valid real value. You define what counts as valid with an `allowed=`
set or a `min_val=` and `max_val=` range, and anything that is neither a documented code nor a valid
value fails. The `score` column has a `-95` that is not in the spec.

```{python}
(
    pb.Validate(data=survey)
    .col_missing_only_coded(columns="score", missing=spec, min_val=0, max_val=100)
    .interrogate()
)
```
